evidence_quotes.quote: I use a logistic regression analysis in order to examine the relationship between theoretically relevant social factors and the probability of a privately owned or operated water system being located within a community.
The dependent variable in this study is the type of entity that owns and operates a water utility system
I coded ownership in the form of a binary variable in order to allow the presence of private water systems to be easily tracked.
As a result, of the 150,669 water utility systems included in the 2012 SDWIS-FED database, only 47,367 are examined here.
To perform the quantitative analysis carried out in this study I utilized a cross-sectional logistic regression on the statistical software package Stata.

criterion_notes.c1: The paper studies community drinking-water utility systems in the United States, but empirically investigates which socioeconomic and demographic factors predict whether a water utility is privately versus publicly owned/operated rather than examining household or community water service access.
criterion_notes.c2: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the paper could be viewed broadly as touching on an institutional/governance factor because water utility privatization (private ownership/operation and public-private partnerships versus public ownership) is an institutional arrangement, although it is modeled here as the dependent variable rather than as an explanatory governance factor. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2, it fails (c2 = no): utility ownership or regulatory structure is eligible only when analyzed as a mechanism directly governing service access, whereas this study models county demographic predictors of utility ownership without examining any rule-type mechanism governing access, tariffs, connections, or exclusions. Because the paper also lacks an eligible service-access outcome (Criterion 4), the overall decision is exclude under both readings.
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical quantitative cross-sectional study using logistic regression on 47,367 U.S. community water systems from the 2012 EPA SDWIS-Fed database linked with 2008-2012 U.S. Census county-level demographic estimates.
criterion_notes.c4: Fails Criterion 4: the sole empirical dependent variable is binary institutional ownership status (whether a community water utility system is privately owned/operated vs. publicly owned). Affordability/rate hikes and water quality failures after privatization are discussed only via secondary literature in the background and are not measured or analyzed as study outcomes.
criterion_notes.c5: Unit of analysis and sample (47,367 U.S. community water systems in 2012), exposures (county unemployment rate, median household income and its square, percent racial minority, percent without a college degree, and log population served), outcome (binary private vs. public ownership/operation), and design (cross-sectional logistic regression) are clearly reported.

population_and_sample: Community water utility systems in the United States from the 2012 EPA Safe Drinking Water Information System (SDWIS-Fed) database merged with 2008-2012 U.S. Census county-level demographic estimates (N = 47,367 community water systems; unit of analysis: water utility system)
exposure: County-level socioeconomic and demographic characteristics (unemployment rate, median household income and quadratic term, percent racial minority, percent without a college degree) and water system characteristics (log population served, geographic region, water source)
outcome: Binary indicator of water utility system privatization (privately owned or operated community water system including public-private partnerships coded as 1 vs. publicly owned water system coded as 0)
rationale: Exclude (E04: Wrong outcome). Although this cross-sectional logistic regression analyzes 47,367 U.S. community water systems and motivates the topic with secondary literature on post-privatization rate increases and water quality problems, its empirical analysis examines county-level socioeconomic and demographic predictors (unemployment, income, race, education, and population served) of whether a water utility is privately owned/operated versus publicly owned. Because institutional ownership status is the dependent variable and no outcome measuring household or community water access, connection, availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion is empirically assessed (nor does the study test how utility ownership rules govern service access), it fails Criteria 1, 2 (narrow reading), and 4, and is excluded under both the narrow and plain readings of Criterion 2.
